patients.summary: Healthy regional sales representative who joined in 2023 and then had three motor vehicle collisions in 15 months: splenic rupture with hemorrhagic shock needing splenectomy (2024), a suspected minor liver injury managed nonoperatively (2025), and a delayed small-bowel perforation with peritonitis needing resection (2026). Asplenia care and vaccines run through primary care.

documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
NEW PATIENT / PREVENTIVE VISIT

27 y/o man here to set up primary care. Sells for a distributor and covers a regional territory, so most of his week is in the car. Last physical was about a year ago at his previous office; he signed a release today for those records. No complaints. Liked the idea of being able to text the office instead of waiting on hold.

PMH: none
PSH: none
Meds: none, no supplements
Allergies: no known drug allergies
FH: nothing he's aware of that runs in the family. Specifically asked: no bleeding problems, no liver disease.
Social: Never smoked, doesn't vape. A drink or two on a weekend, no more than that. No drug use. Single, lives in South Hadley. Lifts at a gym a couple of times a week when his schedule allows.

ROS: 14-point review negative.

Exam: vitals reviewed. Well-appearing, relaxed.
HEENT: TMs and oropharynx clear. Neck: supple, thyroid normal size, no adenopathy.
CV: regular rate, no murmur. Lungs: clear throughout.
Abdomen: soft, nontender, no liver or spleen edge felt.
Skin: no concerning lesions. Ext: warm, no edema. Neuro: alert, moves all four, gait normal.
PHQ-2 0. AUDIT-C 2.

Assessment/plan: healthy 27-year-old establishing care.
- Baseline labs today: CBC, CMP, lipid panel. One-time HIV and hepatitis C screening, he agreed.
- Flu shot given today.
- Tdap: thinks he had one "a few years ago"; will reconcile once outside records come in.
- COVID: plans to get this season's shot at his pharmacy.
- Next physical in a year. Text or call for anything before then.

28M. Nothing new over the past year. Work has been busy; he picked up more accounts and is on the road four days most weeks. Sleeping fine. Still gets to the gym. Alcohol the same, a couple of drinks a week at most. Not taking anything.

conditions.label: Traumatic hemorrhagic shock with acute coagulopathy

reports.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
reports.text: Indication: high-speed MVC, LUQ pain. Technique: axial CT of the abdomen and pelvis after IV contrast, portal venous phase, with multiplanar reformats. Findings: The spleen is lacerated through the hilum with a large-volume hemoperitoneum tracking along both paracolic gutters into the pelvis. Focus of active contrast extravasation at the splenic hilum. The liver enhances homogeneously without laceration. Kidneys, adrenals and pancreas are intact. No bowel wall thickening, no free air. No pelvic or spinal fracture. Lung bases clear.
reports.conclusion: High-grade splenic laceration through the hilum with active extravasation and large hemoperitoneum. No hepatic, renal, pancreatic or bowel injury. No fracture.

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
REGIONAL TRAUMA CENTER - EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT
Date of service: 10/27/2024   Arrival 16:35 via ALS ambulance

CC: highway motor vehicle collision, high speed

HPI: 28-year-old male driver brought in after a high-speed crash. On arrival he was alert, answering questions, with vital signs in an acceptable range, and he complained of pain in the left upper abdomen going up into the left shoulder. CT was obtained during that window. About 30 minutes after arrival he turned pale and sweaty and his pressure dropped to 82/46 with a heart rate of 128. Trauma activation upgraded.

PMH: none. PSH: none. Meds: none. Allergies: NKDA.
FH: noncontributory; no known bleeding disorder or chronic liver disease in the family.
SH: never smoker; drinks socially, 1-2 per week; works in sales.

Primary survey: airway patent, breath sounds equal bilaterally, pulses present but thready after the decline.
Secondary survey: pale, diaphoretic. Abdomen tender with guarding and rebound, maximal in the LUQ. No bruising, lacerations or deformity found; pelvis stable, long bones intact, no fractures on imaging.

FAST (bedside, ED physician): free fluid in the peritoneal cavity.
CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast: see radiology report.

Labs: Hgb 10.4 g/dL, plt 142 K/uL, PT 19.6 s, INR 1.7.

ED course: 2 large-bore IVs, warmed crystalloid bolus. Massive transfusion protocol activated at 17:08; red cells and plasma started in the ED. Trauma surgery at the bedside; patient taken directly to the operating room at 17:24.

Impression:
1. Blunt abdominal trauma with traumatic splenic rupture
2. Hemorrhagic shock with acute traumatic coagulopathy

Disposition: OR with trauma surgery.

medications.drug: acetaminophen 325 MG / oxycodone hydrochloride 5 MG Oral Tablet
medications.sig: Take 1 tablet by mouth every 6 hours as needed for severe pain. Dispense 12 tablets.

procedures.procedure: Hospital discharge day management, 30 minutes or less

documents.title: Operative Report
documents.author: trauma surgery
documents.body:
OPERATIVE REPORT - TRAUMA SURGERY
Date of surgery: 10/27/2024

Preoperative diagnosis: hemoperitoneum with splenic injury, hemorrhagic shock after blunt trauma
Postoperative diagnosis: traumatic splenic rupture through the hilum
Procedure: exploratory laparotomy, splenectomy
Anesthesia: general endotracheal
Blood products (ED and OR, massive transfusion protocol): 6 units packed red cells, 6 units plasma, 1 apheresis platelets

Findings: Approximately 2.5 L of blood and clot evacuated, concentrated in the left upper quadrant. The spleen was fractured across the hilum and bleeding briskly. Liver inspected and intact. Stomach, pancreatic tail and both kidneys without injury. Small and large bowel examined from the ligament of Treitz to the rectum without injury. No retroperitoneal hematoma.

Description: Supine, prepped and draped. Midline laparotomy. Four-quadrant packing. The spleen was mobilized, the hilum clamped and suture-ligated, and the spleen removed. Packs removed sequentially with no further bleeding. Irrigated. Fascia closed with running looped absorbable monofilament, skin with staples.

Condition: hemodynamics improved with resuscitation; extubated in the OR and taken to the surgical ICU.

documents.title: Discharge Summary
documents.author: trauma surgery
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY - TRAUMA SURGERY
Admitted 10/27/2024   Discharged 11/01/2024

Diagnoses:
1. Traumatic splenic rupture, status post exploratory laparotomy and splenectomy 10/27/2024
2. Hemorrhagic shock with acute traumatic coagulopathy, corrected with massive transfusion

Hospital course: Came to us from the ED in shock after a high-speed collision; went straight to the OR for splenectomy (see operative report). One night in the SICU. Coagulation normalized after resuscitation. Hemoglobin low point 7.6 on POD1 and then stable without further transfusion; 9.2 on the day of discharge. Clear liquids POD1, regular diet POD3, flatus and BM by POD3. Walking the halls independently. Pain controlled with oral medication.

Asplenia: he was counseled that he is now at lifelong increased risk of severe infection. Post-splenectomy vaccines (pneumococcal, meningococcal ACWY and B, Hib) not given here; requested that his PCP give them at or after 14 days from surgery.

Allergies: NKDA
Discharge medications: acetaminophen-oxycodone 325/5 mg, 1 tab every 6 hours as needed for severe pain, #12. Over-the-counter acetaminophen otherwise.

Instructions: no lifting over 10 lb. No driving while taking oxycodone. Staple removal at trauma clinic in about two weeks. See PCP within one week. Seek care immediately for fever of 100.4 F or higher.

documents.title: Hospital Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Post-hospital visit

Trauma center discharge summary, operative report and ED record reviewed; they arrived Monday.
Summary: 10/27 he was the driver in a high-speed crash, came in with LUQ and left shoulder pain, became hypotensive in the ED, and went for emergency laparotomy. Spleen was ruptured through the hilum and was removed. Needed massive transfusion for shock with coagulopathy. SICU one night, home 11/1.

Today: incision sore when he gets up from a chair. Has used about half of the oxycodone, only at night, last one Sunday; acetaminophen during the day is enough now. Appetite back. Bowels normal. No fever or chills. Tired by mid-afternoon. Hasn't driven.

Exam: vitals as recorded, afebrile. Tired-appearing but comfortable. Heart regular. Lungs clear. Midline incision with staples in place, edges together, no redness or drainage. Abdomen soft, tender only around the wound. Calves nontender.

CBC: Hgb 10.6 today (9.2 at discharge).

A/P
1. Splenectomy for traumatic splenic rupture. The rupture and the shock are behind him; added asplenia to his problem list in their place. Long talk about what it means: infections can become serious quickly for the rest of his life. A temperature of 100.4 or above, shaking chills or feeling suddenly very ill means calling us the same day or going to an ED, and telling them he has no spleen. Suggested a medical alert bracelet or a note in his phone.
2. Vaccines: due at day 14 or later. Nurse visit 11/12 for PCV20, MenACWY, MenB and Hib, and his flu shot. Second meningococcal doses about 8 weeks after.
3. Hgb climbing. Recheck in about a month.
4. Pain: stop oxycodone; told him to take the leftover tablets to a drop box. Acetaminophen as needed.
5. Work: out until trauma clinic (11/13, staple removal) gives him restrictions.

documents.title: Nurse Visit - Immunizations
documents.author: RN
documents.body:
Here for vaccines per PCP, day 16 after splenectomy. Afebrile. Feels better than last week, no fever since discharge.

Given, 0.5 mL IM each, lots and expirations in the immunization record:
- Prevnar 20, left deltoid
- Menveo (MenACWY), left deltoid, separate site
- Bexsero (MenB-4C), right deltoid
- ActHIB, right deltoid, separate site
- Influenza (trivalent), left deltoid lower site

VIS sheets given. Waited 15 minutes in the office, no reaction. Second Menveo and Bexsero due 8 weeks from today; scheduled 1/14/2025.

documents.author: trauma surgery
documents.body:
Re: Lucas Wisniewski, DOB 05/06/1996
Seen in trauma surgery clinic 11/13/2024

Dear colleague,

Mr. Wisniewski came for his first post-operative visit 17 days after exploratory laparotomy and splenectomy. Pain is mild and he is off opioids. Eating and moving his bowels normally, no fevers. Staples removed today; the incision is healed with no erythema or drainage and no fascial defect.

I am fine with him returning to work on light duty. No lifting over 10 pounds until six weeks from surgery (12/8). Driving is fine now that he is off oxycodone. I see the post-splenectomy vaccines were given 11/12; thank you.

We will see him again on 12/10. NKDA. No medications.

Trauma Surgery

conditions.label: Blunt abdominal trauma with suspected hepatic injury

reports.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
reports.text: Indication: head-on MVC, RUQ tenderness, positive FAST. Prior splenectomy. Technique: portal venous phase CT of the abdomen and pelvis after IV contrast, with coronal and sagittal reformats. Findings: Small, ill-defined hypodensity along the periphery of the right hepatic lobe, segment VI, which may represent a small contusion or laceration. Small amount of fluid around the liver and in the hepatorenal recess. No active contrast extravasation. Spleen surgically absent; no fluid in the splenic bed. Kidneys, pancreas and adrenals normal. Bowel normal in caliber without wall thickening; no free air. No fracture.
reports.conclusion: Possible small contusion or laceration at the edge of the right hepatic lobe (segment VI) with a small amount of perihepatic and hepatorenal fluid. No active extravasation. Postsplenectomy. No other injury.

REGIONAL TRAUMA CENTER - EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT
Date of service: 05/17/2025   Arrival 14:20 by ambulance

CC: car crash

HPI: 29M, belted driver, head-on collision this afternoon. Known to our trauma service: splenectomy in October 2024 after a splenic rupture from an earlier collision, roughly seven months ago. Complains of right upper abdominal pain. Alert and oriented x3, anxious, keeps asking whether he'll need surgery again.

PMH: asplenia after traumatic splenectomy. PSH: exploratory laparotomy with splenectomy, 10/2024. Meds: none. Allergies: NKDA.
FH: noncontributory, no bleeding disorders or liver disease. SH: never smoker, 1-2 drinks a week, sales rep.

Vitals: BP 130/85, HR 95, RR 18, SpO2 98% RA.
Exam: no abrasions, contusions or seatbelt mark. Chest wall nontender, breath sounds equal. Abdomen: tender in the RUQ with voluntary guarding; no rebound. Healed midline scar. Pelvis stable. Neuro intact.

FAST: fluid in Morison's pouch.
Labs: Hgb 13.2, Hct 39.5, plt 250 K. Liver enzymes and bilirubin normal.
CT A/P with contrast: possible small right-lobe liver contusion/laceration, small perihepatic and hepatorenal fluid, no extravasation (radiology report attached).

MDM: blunt abdominal trauma with suspected hepatic injury. Hemodynamically normal, no active bleeding on CT. Nonoperative management appropriate. Discussed with trauma surgery.

Disposition: admit to trauma surgery for observation, serial abdominal exams and hemoglobins.

medications.sig: Take 1 tablet by mouth every 6 hours as needed for pain. No more than 3,000 mg in 24 hours.

documents.title: Discharge Summary
documents.author: trauma surgery
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY - TRAUMA SURGERY (observation)
Admitted 05/17/2025   Discharged 05/19/2025

Diagnosis: blunt abdominal trauma with suspected hepatic injury (possible small segment VI contusion/laceration on CT), managed nonoperatively.
Other: asplenia after splenectomy 10/2024.

Course: Observed on the trauma floor with serial exams. Hemodynamics normal throughout. Hemoglobin 13.2 on arrival, 12.9 overnight, 13.0 this morning. RUQ tenderness eased, guarding gone by day 2. Diet resumed without nausea. Walking independently. No fevers.

Allergies: NKDA
Discharge medication: acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed, maximum 3 g per day.

Instructions: no heavy lifting, contact sports or strenuous exercise for 4 weeks. Return for worsening abdominal pain, dizziness, shortness of breath, or any fever (asplenic). Trauma clinic in about 3 weeks. PCP within one week.

events.reason: Follow-up after ED visit and observation stay

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Post-ED Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
F/u after trauma center ED and 2-night observation (records received 5/21 and reviewed).

Head-on crash 5/17, belted driver. RUQ pain, FAST positive in Morison's pouch, CT with a possible small contusion or laceration at the edge of the right liver lobe, no active bleeding. Hgb 13.2 -> 12.9 -> 13.0. Watched and sent home 5/19.

Now: right-sided ache mostly gone. Took acetaminophen twice the first day home and none since Tuesday. No fever, no dizziness. Eating normally. Urine and stools normal color.

Exam: afebrile, vitals normal. No scleral icterus. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, minimal tenderness in the RUQ without guarding. Old midline scar healed.

A/P
Blunt abdominal trauma with suspected small liver injury, nonoperative, improving as expected.
- No need to keep acetaminophen on his list; can use OTC if the ache returns.
- Activity per trauma: nothing strenuous or heavy until mid-June. Trauma clinic 6/11.
- Reviewed again: as an asplenic patient any fever gets same-day attention.
- Out of work until Tuesday, then back to his usual job; he says he doesn't need a letter this time.

REGIONAL TRAUMA CENTER - EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT
Date of service: 01/15/2026   Arrival 13:05

CC: severe abdominal pain

HPI: 29M with prior traumatic splenic rupture (splenectomy 10/2024) and blunt abdominal trauma with a suspected liver injury (observed here 5/2025), both from earlier car crashes. Two days ago he was in another collision with a seatbelt mark across the lower abdomen; seen at an outside ED, CT reportedly unremarkable, sent home. About 4 hours ago he had abrupt onset of sharp, constant lower abdominal pain that has gotten steadily worse. Denies nausea or vomiting; bowel habits unchanged.

PSH: exploratory laparotomy with splenectomy 10/2024. Meds: none. Allergies: NKDA.
FH: noncontributory; no bleeding disorders or liver disease. SH: never smoker, social alcohol, sales.

Vitals: BP 100/60, HR 120, RR 22, T 37.8 C.
Exam: uncomfortable, lying still. Abdomen with diffuse tenderness, rebound and guarding; bowel sounds hypoactive. Fading seatbelt bruise across the lower abdomen. Old midline scar.

Labs: WBC 15.0 K/uL, Hgb 13.2 g/dL, lactate 3.5 mmol/L.
Upright chest film: free air under the diaphragm.

Impression: hollow viscus perforation with peritonitis after blunt trauma, most likely small bowel.
ED course: 2 L crystalloid, IV piperacillin-tazobactam, IV analgesia. Surgery at bedside; to OR.

medications.drug: acetaminophen 325 MG / oxycodone hydrochloride 5 MG Oral Tablet
medications.sig: Take 1 tablet by mouth every 6 hours as needed for severe pain. Dispense 12 tablets.

reports.text: Specimen: small intestine, ileum, segmental resection. Gross: segment of small bowel 12 cm in length with stapled ends, a full-thickness defect on the antimesenteric wall and fibrinous exudate on the serosa. Microscopic: transmural defect with acute inflammation and necrosis at the edges; acute fibrinopurulent serositis. Mucosa away from the defect unremarkable. Both stapled margins viable.
reports.conclusion: Small intestine (ileum), resection: transmural perforation with acute serositis. Margins viable.

procedures.procedure: Hospital discharge day management, 30 minutes or less

documents.title: Operative Report
documents.author: trauma surgery
documents.body:
OPERATIVE REPORT - TRAUMA / ACUTE CARE SURGERY
Date of surgery: 01/15/2026

Preoperative diagnosis: pneumoperitoneum and peritonitis after blunt abdominal trauma
Postoperative diagnosis: traumatic perforation of the ileum with secondary peritonitis
Procedure: re-exploratory laparotomy, segmental small-bowel resection with stapled primary anastomosis, abdominal washout
Anesthesia: general

Findings: Enteric contents and fibrinous exudate throughout the lower abdomen and pelvis. Full-thickness perforation of the ileum about 60 cm proximal to the ileocecal valve. Remaining small bowel and colon examined end to end without other injury. Liver unremarkable. Splenic bed clean.

Description: Entry through the prior midline incision. Contamination evacuated and cultures not sent. The injured segment, about 12 cm, was resected with a stapler and a side-to-side functional end-to-end stapled anastomosis created; mesenteric defect closed. Abdomen irrigated with several liters of warm saline until clear. Fascia closed with running looped absorbable suture; skin closed with staples over wicks.

To the floor in stable condition.

documents.title: Discharge Summary
documents.author: trauma surgery
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY - TRAUMA / ACUTE CARE SURGERY
Admitted 01/15/2026   Discharged 01/21/2026

Diagnosis: traumatic perforation of the small intestine (ileum) with secondary peritonitis, 2 days after a seatbelt injury.
Procedure: re-laparotomy, 12 cm ileal resection with primary anastomosis, washout (01/15).
Other: asplenia after splenectomy 10/2024.

Course: Piperacillin-tazobactam IV for 4 days after source control, then stopped. Afebrile from POD2. Diet advanced from POD3 with return of bowel function; tolerating a regular diet on discharge. Walking independently. Wound clean; wicks out POD2. Pathology: transmural perforation with acute serositis, viable margins.

Allergies: NKDA
Discharge medications: acetaminophen-oxycodone 325/5 mg 1 tab every 6 hours as needed for severe pain, #12; acetaminophen otherwise.

Instructions: no lifting over 10 lb until early March. No driving on oxycodone. Staples out at surgery clinic 2/4. PCP within a week. Any fever, vomiting, worsening pain or wound drainage: return.

medications.drug: acetaminophen 325 MG / oxycodone hydrochloride 5 MG Oral Tablet

documents.title: Hospital Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Post-discharge visit. Records from both EDs, the op note, pathology and discharge summary came in Friday; reviewed.

Course: MVC 1/13 with a seatbelt bruise, outside ED CT negative, sent home. Two days later sudden severe lower abdominal pain; trauma center found free air and peritonitis; re-laparotomy 1/15 with a 12 cm ileal resection and primary anastomosis for a perforation. 4 days of pip-tazo. Home 1/21.

Today: eating three small meals plus snacks, no nausea. Bowel movements daily, soft. No fevers. Incision tight but improving. Took oxycodone the first two nights home only; acetaminophen since. Down about 4 kg from his usual.

Exam: afebrile, vitals stable, weight 78 kg. Comfortable. Lungs clear, heart regular. Midline incision with staples, clean and dry, no erythema or drainage. Abdomen soft, appropriately tender near the wound, not distended, bowel sounds normal.

CBC: WBC 8.4, Hgb 12.6.

A/P
1. Traumatic small-bowel perforation with peritonitis, s/p resection: recovering well. WBC normal. Staples out at surgery clinic 2/4. Eat as tolerated; weight should come back.
2. Pain: off oxycodone; removed from his list.
3. Asplenia: MenB booster was due this month. Holding until he's further out from surgery; nurse visit in March.
4. Work: will message when surgery clears him for desk and driving duties.
